summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. summary: This record contains the source code, trained models, and derived research artifacts associated with the study “Physical fidelity and forecasting in compressed active matter representations.” The study evaluates how dimensionality reduction affects spatial reconstruction, physical fidelity, and temporal forecasting in active-matter simulations. It compares unconstrained, physics-constrained, realizability-constrained, and combined autoencoders with proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), at latent dimensions of 128, 256, and 512. Forecasting comparisons include linear autoregression, multilayer perceptrons, and persistence baselines. Reconstruction accuracy, physical admissibility, and forecast performance are treated as distinct evaluation objectives. The archive includes: • Source code for data acquisition, representation training, posthoc analysis, frozen final evaluation, and publication rendering. • Scientific configurations and dependency specifications. • Selected trained checkpoints, POD models, fitted forecasters, latent caches, training histories, and validation analyses. • Frozen final-test outputs, comparison summaries, coverage diagnostics, and provenance records. • Numerical visual exports, software tests, and workflow documentation. The original simulation data were downloaded from The Well, specifically its active_matter dataset. We acknowledge the original simulation contributors and the developers and curators of The Well. The original HDF5 simulation files are not redistributed in this record; the repository documents their acquisition, pinned revision, and content-hash verification. The Well: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/ Associated publication: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00568 Dataset documentation: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/datasets/active_matter/ Last-epoch checkpoints named last.pt are excluded; selected best.pt checkpoints are retained. Publication figures, tables, numerical source data, and supplementary videos are supplied with the manuscript submission and are excluded from this archive. Their public availability follows the release of the article and its supplementary materials. The code for generating those outputs remains included. The deposited ZIP contains 1,534 files and occupies approximately 26.18 GB. The accompanying README provides the archive’s SHA-256 checksum, a contents guide, installation references, and verification limits. Packaging integrity and source-checksum checks do not constitute an independent full-data replication. Some archived provenance records retain original execution paths; independent reruns should use a separate work directory and preserve the frozen results. Development repository: https://github.com/BioDecodingLab/Physically_Constrained_Representations_of_Active_Matter

summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. WARP Versioning and Releasing Pipelines in WARP are versioned semantically to support reproducibility in scientific analysis and provide clearer analysis provenance. Version numbers allow researchers to confirm their data has all been processed in a compati

Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. WARP Versioning and Releasing Pipelines in WARP are versioned semantically to support reproducibility in scientific analysis and provide clearer analysis provenance. summary: ENERGY DISTRIBUTION IN INTELLIGENT ROBOTIC MATTER AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:智能機器人物質能源分配極限 21/90 ENERGY DISTRIBUTION IN INTELLIGENT ROBOTIC MATTER AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition of STARLI's YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy, asking whether twenty-four locally controlled robotic-matter modules can share a bounded energy supply for a fixed, verified vehicle-body reconfiguration task without concealing external work, structural risk or unsafe communication delays. The three-coupling is Energy Networks x Distributed Power Supply x Vehicle Reconfiguration. Tests are restricted to unoccupied, scaled hardware, traceable electrical rails and laboratory/hardware-in-the-loop environments; no completed roadworthy or nanorobotic supercar is claimed. The falsifiable hypothesis is that a pre-registered distributed allocator can reduce total mission joules at the same useful task, material mass, sensing quality, energy sources, cooling, computation, time and operator budget as a properly optimized wired centralized architecture, while not worsening critical command latency. A hidden unmetered driver, local thermal hotspot, power-rail partition, stale packets, reserve deficit or failure of physical stopping defeats the claim. The supplied consensus model, dx_i/dt = -sum_j a_ij(x_i-x_j)+w_i, is used to study local agreement; agreement alone cannot prove charge conservation, battery state of charge or safe power distribution. Thirty distinct mathematical research plates examine energy-balance and signed-work integration, nodal current conservation, converter and contact losses, motor work, SOC integration and transient terminal voltage, resistor networks, rated-edge loading, droop sharing, negative incremental impedance, spectral connectivity, packet age, deadline reliability, thermal RC and Joule heating, dependent hazards, stop-energy reserve, constrained dispatch, worst-node tail risk, covariance propagation and physical safe-stop latency. Each plate provides mathematical or physical construction, dimensional limits, an individually specified blind challenge and chapter references. Across eighty-two chapters and 410 single-page investigations, the research program spans power-source custody, reconfigurable conductors, communication and consensus, electrothermal safety, fault isolation and independent qualification. Two hundred Research Gates pose distinct concealed-fault, equal-resource competitor and cross-interface problems with separate challenge, rival and stopping explanations. Thirty-three different Phoenix Answer Embryos propose experimental meters, isolation benches, duty referees, communication-energy witnesses, thermal artifacts and second-laboratory transfer contracts. These are hypothesis-forming research proposals, not completed devices or demonstrated physical outcomes. The DOI ancestry preserves author-supplied parent identifiers 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318839 (metadata not independently confirmed). External component and methodology references include Robo-Matter (10.1038/s41467-024-53123-6), flying-swarm shape assembly (10.1038/s44172-026-00715-3), adaptive magnetic microrobots (10.1038/s41427-026-00682-3), changing-topology consensus (10.1109/TAC.2005.846556), distributed power sharing (10.1109/TPWRD.2012.2212919), energy-aware multi-robot allocation (10.1016/j.robot.2024.104762), and wireless robotic power transfer (10.1049/csy2.70065). These studies support limited component analogies and methods; none proves the integrated F21 vehicle-body architecture, passenger safety or nanoscale-to-macroscopic feasibility. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. summary: SAOS 6.0.0 This release brings tomographic control for MCAO, a redesigned deformable-mirror model, more accurate wavefront sensors and imaging, and a validation suite that compares every module with theory. From now on, a release to master requires the validation suite to pass. Highlights Tomographic reconstruction (Learn & Apply) with an atmospheric-profile estimator: Cn², r0, L0, wind, noise. Includes predictive L&A and joint reconstruction for several WFSs and DMs. Deformable mirrors with partition-of-unity influence functions , support for custom influence functions and DM dynamic models. Wavefront sensors: partially illuminated subapertures, with pupil amplitude and phase interpolation; continuous thresholded centre of gravity. Science camera: the PSF is computed by a matrix Fourier transform on the native pupil sampling, limited to its Nyquist band; no phase interpolation is involved; SAOS reports the resolution needed to cover the whole field. Validation suite and release gate: physics-based tests in tiers (fast, nightly), an HTML report and a GitHub check on a self-hosted runner that a pull request to master must pass. Solar images on Zenodo: downloaded on demand and verified by checksum. Git LFS is no longer needed. Documentation: every module page explains its theory and implementation, with equations and references. There is also a validation catalogue describing each test, its assumptions and tolerances. Control and reconstruction Learn & Apply tomography (standard and predictive), with a learning stage that estimates: the turbulence profile (fractional Cn², r0, L0) from the slope covariances, using analytical von Kármán covariances; the wind of each layer; the WFS noise. Reconstructors: Tikhonov-regularised reconstructors; joint interaction matrix for several WFSs and DMs, inverted as a single system; target residuals driven to zero by DM cooperation. Control laws: leaky integrator, generic state-space controller and pseudo-open-loop control (POLC). In per-DM POLC, the pseudo-open-loop slopes of each WFS include the contribution of every DM that it sees. Modal bases: zonal, Zernike, KL, Hadamard and Disk Harmonics. summary: Real Analysis Volume 1: Foundations of Real Analysis , authored by Helbert Justo Luque Zevallos and published by Proyecto Ágora as part of the Undergraduate Mathematics Series , is a university-level academic textbook devoted to the logical, algebraic, and axiomatic foundations of real analysis. The book provides a systematic and rigorous introduction to mathematical reasoning, formal proof techniques, and the fundamental structure of the real number system. Its primary objective is to develop the conceptual understanding and mathematical maturity required for advanced undergraduate studies in mathematical analysis. Chapter 1: Mathematical Language and Proof Techniques This chapter introduces propositional logic, logical connectives, truth tables, implications, equivalences, universal and existential quantifiers, and the negation of quantified statements. It develops the theory of sets, equivalence and order relations, injective, surjective, and bijective functions, images, preimages, composition, and inverse functions. Particular emphasis is placed on direct proof, proof by contraposition, proof by contradiction, mathematical induction, and the construction of counterexamples. The chapter also examines rigorous mathematical writing, common logical errors, finite and infinite sets, countability, and the uncountability of the real numbers. Chapter 2: The Real Number System The second chapter develops the axiomatic structure of the real numbers through field axioms, order axioms, and the compatibility of algebraic operations with order. It examines absolute value, the triangle inequality, fundamental inequalities, intervals, neighborhoods, upper and lower bounds, suprema, infima, maxima, and minima. A central component is the completeness property of the real numbers , including the structural distinction between rational and real numbers, the Archimedean property, the density of rational and irrational numbers, and the nested interval theorem. The chapter concludes with significant consequences of completeness, including the existence of roots, rational approximations, the supremum principle as a mathematical proof technique, and the relationship between completeness and convergence. Pedagogical Approach The textbook integrates precise definitions, propositions, lemmas, theorems, complete mathematical proofs, explanatory examples, and carefully constructed counterexamples. It includes 120 fully solved exercises and 150 proposed exercises , organized according to the main topics of the two chapters. These activities reinforce theoretical understanding, logical reasoning, mathematical writing, and independent problem-solving skills. Intended Audience This publication is intended for undergraduate mathematics students, university instructors, mathematics educators, and independent learners seeking a rigorous foundation in real analysis. As the first volume of a six-volume academic collection, it establishes the theoretical and methodological foundations for subsequent studies of sequences, numerical series, limits, continuity, metric spaces, compactness, differential calculus, Riemann integration, uniform convergence, and differential equations. summary: THERMAL MANAGEMENT OF MORPHING ROBOTIC VEHICLE BODIES AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:可變形車體的熱管理極限 22/90 THERMAL MANAGEMENT OF MORPHING ROBOTIC VEHICLE BODIES AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition in STARLI's YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy, asking whether a scaled morphing robotic vehicle-body section can redistribute heat without hiding interface hotspots, temperature-induced material degradation or cooling-energy costs. Its three-coupling is Heat Conduction x Distributed Actuation x Thermal Safety. The program is restricted to 24-module unoccupied bench assemblies, coupons, sealed thermal chambers and hardware-in-the-loop control. It makes no claim of a road-ready vehicle, passenger protection or independently demonstrated nanoscale-to-macroscopic performance. The falsifiable candidate compares a frozen morphology-aware heat-management policy against equally resourced fixed passive and centralized wired thermal designs. Under matched mechanical tasks, material mass, source heat, cooling-work budget, sensing access and mission duration, the candidate should reduce the worst qualified local temperature without worsening safety-critical deadline-valid packet survival. The preassigned model rank([C;CA;...;CA^(n-1)])=n tests observability of an ideal local linear state representation; it does not itself prove physical temperature correctness. A hidden heat source, emissivity shift, detached thermal bridge, blocked coolant, over-temperature joint, unaccounted fan input, undercovered uncertainty or ineffective physical stop defeats release. summary: Coarse flood maps support regional risk assessment but omit terrain detail relevant to local exposure. We present floodsr, a Python framework for reconstructing fine-grid flood depths using a trained residual U-Net (ResUNet) or the existing terrain-based CostGrow method. We trained the terrain-conditioned ResUNet on paired Canadian hydraulic simulations and evaluated it on withheld spatial tiles and independent simulations at two external sites. Wet-loss training improved reconstruction on five selected tiles, although internal validation favoured the deployed baseline. External depth errors decreased, but wet-depth errors and spatial agreement did not improve consistently. CPU benchmarks quantified runtime and memory for both methods, and repeatability and input-validation checks passed in the tested configurations. The framework supports comparison and reuse of reconstruction methods; application-specific validation remains necessary because finer grids do not guarantee more accurate flood maps.   Non-peer-reviewed preprint. Includes the manuscript and supplementary material. Software: https://github.com/cefect/floodsr . Documentation: https://floodsr.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ .
title: floodsr: A lightweight Python toolkit for terrain-conditioned flood map super-resolution

summary: 智能機器人物質驅動的自主底盤極限 13/90 ROBOTIC-MATTER-DRIVEN AUTONOMOUS CHASSIS AT THE LIMIT ROBOTIC-MATTER-DRIVEN AUTONOMOUS CHASSIS AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page high-density English research working monograph examining whether a chassis made from interacting robotic-matter modules can reversibly change its load-bearing geometry without losing structural integrity, traction confidence, actuator authority or independently reconstructable state identity. Its scope is limited to unoccupied, scaled rigs and falsifiable engineering research. Its principal hypothesis can be refuted. With equivalent materials, mass, testing time, energy, sensing and control resources, a preregistered adaptive chassis should improve traction reserve without worsening energy per mission, path error, or structural stability relative to a well-tuned fixed-geometry chassis and conservative rule-based controller. Apparent gains that vanish under actuator, controller or load-path ablations cannot be attributed to robotic matter. Thirty mathematical and physical research plates address six-degree dynamic balance, graph rigidity, stiffness and failure modes, contact-force closure, structural interface stress, fatigue, consensus, latency, support margins, power accounting, sensor covariance, fault identification and noncompensatory release. Each plate defines units, validity assumptions, an independent physical counter-test and links to substantive chapter investigations. Across 82 chapters and 410 single-page studies, the volume develops mechanical architectures, connector physics, reversible stiffness, decentralized actuation, ground interaction, reference metrology, energy integrity, wear, fair baselines and independent qualification. Two hundred Research Gates frame specific blinded perturbations, rival explanations and hard stopping conditions. Thirty-three different Phoenix Answer Embryos propose distinct tools, diagnostic instruments and successor-ready verification interfaces. This book is hypothesis-generating. It does not report a completed STARLI chassis experiment, nanoscale vehicle manufacturing, quantum superiority or passenger-safe operation. Unknown traction, unstable support, unverifiable mechanical locking, reference invalidity or revoked physical authority require stopping and withholding conclusions. Competing laboratories are invited to reproduce, refute and improve the proposals while keeping failed experiments visible. summary: This record contains the source code, trained models, and derived research artifacts associated with the study “Physical fidelity and forecasting in compressed active matter representations.” The study evaluates how dimensionality reduction affects spatial reconstruction, physical fidelity, and temporal forecasting in active-matter simulations. It compares unconstrained, physics-constrained, realizability-constrained, and combined autoencoders with proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), at latent dimensions of 128, 256, and 512. Forecasting comparisons include linear autoregression, multilayer perceptrons, and persistence baselines. Reconstruction accuracy, physical admissibility, and forecast performance are treated as distinct evaluation objectives. The archive includes: • Source code for data acquisition, representation training, posthoc analysis, frozen final evaluation, and publication rendering. • Scientific configurations and dependency specifications. • Selected trained checkpoints, POD models, fitted forecasters, latent caches, training histories, and validation analyses. • Frozen final-test outputs, comparison summaries, coverage diagnostics, and provenance records. • Numerical visual exports, software tests, and workflow documentation. The original simulation data were downloaded from The Well, specifically its active_matter dataset. We acknowledge the original simulation contributors and the developers and curators of The Well. The original HDF5 simulation files are not redistributed in this record; the repository documents their acquisition, pinned revision, and content-hash verification. The Well: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/ Associated publication: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00568 Dataset documentation: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/datasets/active_matter/ Last-epoch checkpoints named last.pt are excluded; selected best.pt checkpoints are retained. Publication figures, tables, numerical source data, and supplementary videos are supplied with the manuscript submission and are excluded from this archive. Their public availability follows the release of the article and its supplementary materials. The code for generating those outputs remains included. The deposited ZIP contains 1,534 files and occupies approximately 26.18 GB. The accompanying README provides the archive’s SHA-256 checksum, a contents guide, installation references, and verification limits. Packaging integrity and source-checksum checks do not constitute an independent full-data replication. Some archived provenance records retain original execution paths; independent reruns should use a separate work directory and preserve the frozen results. Development repository: https://github.com/BioDecodingLab/Physically_Constrained_Representations_of_Active_Matter

summary: ENERGY DISTRIBUTION IN INTELLIGENT ROBOTIC MATTER AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:智能機器人物質能源分配極限 21/90 ENERGY DISTRIBUTION IN INTELLIGENT ROBOTIC MATTER AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition of STARLI's YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy, asking whether twenty-four locally controlled robotic-matter modules can share a bounded energy supply for a fixed, verified vehicle-body reconfiguration task without concealing external work, structural risk or unsafe communication delays. The three-coupling is Energy Networks x Distributed Power Supply x Vehicle Reconfiguration. Tests are restricted to unoccupied, scaled hardware, traceable electrical rails and laboratory/hardware-in-the-loop environments; no completed roadworthy or nanorobotic supercar is claimed. The falsifiable hypothesis is that a pre-registered distributed allocator can reduce total mission joules at the same useful task, material mass, sensing quality, energy sources, cooling, computation, time and operator budget as a properly optimized wired centralized architecture, while not worsening critical command latency. A hidden unmetered driver, local thermal hotspot, power-rail partition, stale packets, reserve deficit or failure of physical stopping defeats the claim. The supplied consensus model, dx_i/dt = -sum_j a_ij(x_i-x_j)+w_i, is used to study local agreement; agreement alone cannot prove charge conservation, battery state of charge or safe power distribution. Thirty distinct mathematical research plates examine energy-balance and signed-work integration, nodal current conservation, converter and contact losses, motor work, SOC integration and transient terminal voltage, resistor networks, rated-edge loading, droop sharing, negative incremental impedance, spectral connectivity, packet age, deadline reliability, thermal RC and Joule heating, dependent hazards, stop-energy reserve, constrained dispatch, worst-node tail risk, covariance propagation and physical safe-stop latency. Each plate provides mathematical or physical construction, dimensional limits, an individually specified blind challenge and chapter references. Across eighty-two chapters and 410 single-page investigations, the research program spans power-source custody, reconfigurable conductors, communication and consensus, electrothermal safety, fault isolation and independent qualification. Two hundred Research Gates pose distinct concealed-fault, equal-resource competitor and cross-interface problems with separate challenge, rival and stopping explanations. Thirty-three different Phoenix Answer Embryos propose experimental meters, isolation benches, duty referees, communication-energy witnesses, thermal artifacts and second-laboratory transfer contracts. These are hypothesis-forming research proposals, not completed devices or demonstrated physical outcomes. The DOI ancestry preserves author-supplied parent identifiers 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318839 (metadata not independently confirmed). External component and methodology references include Robo-Matter (10.1038/s41467-024-53123-6), flying-swarm shape assembly (10.1038/s44172-026-00715-3), adaptive magnetic microrobots (10.1038/s41427-026-00682-3), changing-topology consensus (10.1109/TAC.2005.846556), distributed power sharing (10.1109/TPWRD.2012.2212919), energy-aware multi-robot allocation (10.1016/j.robot.2024.104762), and wireless robotic power transfer (10.1049/csy2.70065). These studies support limited component analogies and methods; none proves the integrated F21 vehicle-body architecture, passenger safety or nanoscale-to-macroscopic feasibility. summary: SAOS 6.0.0 This release brings tomographic control for MCAO, a redesigned deformable-mirror model, more accurate wavefront sensors and imaging, and a validation suite that compares every module with theory. From now on, a release to master requires the validation suite to pass. Highlights Tomographic reconstruction (Learn & Apply) with an atmospheric-profile estimator: Cn², r0, L0, wind, noise. Includes predictive L&A and joint reconstruction for several WFSs and DMs. Deformable mirrors with partition-of-unity influence functions , support for custom influence functions and DM dynamic models. Wavefront sensors: partially illuminated subapertures, with pupil amplitude and phase interpolation; continuous thresholded centre of gravity. Science camera: the PSF is computed by a matrix Fourier transform on the native pupil sampling, limited to its Nyquist band; no phase interpolation is involved; SAOS reports the resolution needed to cover the whole field. Validation suite and release gate: physics-based tests in tiers (fast, nightly), an HTML report and a GitHub check on a self-hosted runner that a pull request to master must pass. Solar images on Zenodo: downloaded on demand and verified by checksum. Git LFS is no longer needed. Documentation: every module page explains its theory and implementation, with equations and references. There is also a validation catalogue describing each test, its assumptions and tolerances. Control and reconstruction Learn & Apply tomography (standard and predictive), with a learning stage that estimates: the turbulence profile (fractional Cn², r0, L0) from the slope covariances, using analytical von Kármán covariances; the wind of each layer; the WFS noise. Reconstructors: Tikhonov-regularised reconstructors; joint interaction matrix for several WFSs and DMs, inverted as a single system; target residuals driven to zero by DM cooperation. Control laws: leaky integrator, generic state-space controller and pseudo-open-loop control (POLC). In per-DM POLC, the pseudo-open-loop slopes of each WFS include the contribution of every DM that it sees. Modal bases: zonal, Zernike, KL, Hadamard and Disk Harmonics. Piston-free bases have exactly nValidAct − 1 modes. Zernike signs follow Noll. Tip/tilt are removed from altitude DMs. Interaction matrices: DM identity is checked; IM files record their basis convention; files are never appended to: an existing file requires overwrite=True , and the write is atomic; check_output_file() validates the path before a long measurement; identical DMs and light paths reuse the same IM. Scalability: chunked reconstruction and tomography on the GPU, with automatic fallback to the CPU when the matrices do not fit; reduced VRAM use; a common thread pool to avoid CPU oversubscription. Deformable mirrors Partition-of-unity normalised RBF influence functions, and user-supplied influence functions. Misregistration (shift, rotation, radial scaling) applied at the actuator level through the influence functions, so it introduces no interpolation effects. Dynamic response: discrete state-space DM models. Validated against an independent Matlab simulation, including closed-loop timing. Also validated on the sensitivity function for a Tip disturbance of known PSD. Wavefront sensing and imaging Shack-Hartmann: partially illuminated subapertures, with pupil amplitude and normalised phase interpolation and a validity threshold; continuous thresholded centre of gravity; validated use_brightest . Correlating Shack-Hartmann: consistent units in rad or px; flux scaled with the field of view; lower VRAM use. Science camera: matrix Fourier transform on the native pupil sampling, band-limited to the Nyquist band (Whittaker–Shannon); frames produced at the end of each decimation window; long exposures always last at least the requested integration time; an option saves only the long exposure. summary: Real Analysis Volume 1: Foundations of Real Analysis , authored by Helbert Justo Luque Zevallos and published by Proyecto Ágora as part of the Undergraduate Mathematics Series , is a university-level academic textbook devoted to the logical, algebraic, and axiomatic foundations of real analysis. The book provides a systematic and rigorous introduction to mathematical reasoning, formal proof techniques, and the fundamental structure of the real number system. Its primary objective is to develop the conceptual understanding and mathematical maturity required for advanced undergraduate studies in mathematical analysis. Chapter 1: Mathematical Language and Proof Techniques This chapter introduces propositional logic, logical connectives, truth tables, implications, equivalences, universal and existential quantifiers, and the negation of quantified statements. It develops the theory of sets, equivalence and order relations, injective, surjective, and bijective functions, images, preimages, composition, and inverse functions. Particular emphasis is placed on direct proof, proof by contraposition, proof by contradiction, mathematical induction, and the construction of counterexamples. The chapter also examines rigorous mathematical writing, common logical errors, finite and infinite sets, countability, and the uncountability of the real numbers. Chapter 2: The Real Number System The second chapter develops the axiomatic structure of the real numbers through field axioms, order axioms, and the compatibility of algebraic operations with order. It examines absolute value, the triangle inequality, fundamental inequalities, intervals, neighborhoods, upper and lower bounds, suprema, infima, maxima, and minima. A central component is the completeness property of the real numbers , including the structural distinction between rational and real numbers, the Archimedean property, the density of rational and irrational numbers, and the nested interval theorem. The chapter concludes with significant consequences of completeness, including the existence of roots, rational approximations, the supremum principle as a mathematical proof technique, and the relationship between completeness and convergence. Pedagogical Approach The textbook integrates precise definitions, propositions, lemmas, theorems, complete mathematical proofs, explanatory examples, and carefully constructed counterexamples. It includes 120 fully solved exercises and 150 proposed exercises , organized according to the main topics of the two chapters. These activities reinforce theoretical understanding, logical reasoning, mathematical writing, and independent problem-solving skills. Intended Audience This publication is intended for undergraduate mathematics students, university instructors, mathematics educators, and independent learners seeking a rigorous foundation in real analysis. As the first volume of a six-volume academic collection, it establishes the theoretical and methodological foundations for subsequent studies of sequences, numerical series, limits, continuity, metric spaces, compactness, differential calculus, Riemann integration, uniform convergence, and differential equations. summary: THERMAL MANAGEMENT OF MORPHING ROBOTIC VEHICLE BODIES AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:可變形車體的熱管理極限 22/90 THERMAL MANAGEMENT OF MORPHING ROBOTIC VEHICLE BODIES AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition in STARLI's YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy, asking whether a scaled morphing robotic vehicle-body section can redistribute heat without hiding interface hotspots, temperature-induced material degradation or cooling-energy costs. Its three-coupling is Heat Conduction x Distributed Actuation x Thermal Safety. The program is restricted to 24-module unoccupied bench assemblies, coupons, sealed thermal chambers and hardware-in-the-loop control. It makes no claim of a road-ready vehicle, passenger protection or independently demonstrated nanoscale-to-macroscopic performance. The falsifiable candidate compares a frozen morphology-aware heat-management policy against equally resourced fixed passive and centralized wired thermal designs. Under matched mechanical tasks, material mass, source heat, cooling-work budget, sensing access and mission duration, the candidate should reduce the worst qualified local temperature without worsening safety-critical deadline-valid packet survival. The preassigned model rank([C;CA;...;CA^(n-1)])=n tests observability of an ideal local linear state representation; it does not itself prove physical temperature correctness. A hidden heat source, emissivity shift, detached thermal bridge, blocked coolant, over-temperature joint, unaccounted fan input, undercovered uncertainty or ineffective physical stop defeats release. Thirty mathematically distinct research plates address thermal control-volume energy conservation, Fourier and anisotropic conduction, pressure-dependent contact resistance, radiation, convection, dynamic heat storage, resistive heating, actuator dissipation, thermomechanical damage, strain-sensitive thermal conductivity, latent-heat buffering, thermal fatigue, forced cooling, heat-pipe and thermoelectric limits, observability, state-estimator innovation, correlated thermal uncertainty, inverse source ambiguity, physical stop latency, hazard dependence, extreme-tail qualification and Biot/Fourier scale arguments. Every plate specifies construction, dimensions, validity conditions, a separate blind falsification and chapter interfaces. Eighty-two research chapters contain 410 separate single-page investigations into physical heat source truth, changing morphology and thermal contacts, sparse sensor observability, cooling systems, thermally induced damage and second-site qualification. Two hundred Research Gates contain individually anchored hidden-fault, matched-comparator and cross-chapter questions with specific scientific notes and stopping criteria. Thirty-three distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos propose instruments, calorimeters, thermal-refusal cards, contact-heat probes, material aging tests and successor negative-case archives. These are prospective research designs, not completed results or operating vehicle hardware. Reference ancestry includes the author's supplied Flagship 13 identifiers 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318839 (metadata not independently confirmed). External peer-reviewed component literature includes Robo-Matter (10.1038/s41467-024-53123-6), thermally switchable polymers (10.1038/s41467-024-49354-2), thermally actuated soft robotics (10.1002/adma.202504683), conductive elastomer films (10.1039/D5NR03526K), responsive battery thermal regulation (10.1038/s41560-024-01535-5), phase-change/heat-pipe cooling (10.1016/j.enconman.2024.118506), and the supplied 2026 swarm/microrobot references (10.1038/s44172-026-00715-3; 10.1038/s41427-026-00682-3). Publications support component hypotheses and measurement methods; none independently verifies the integrated F22 concept. Author: Feng Cheng-en (33) x STARLI / Xingli Series: STARLI Research Institute XXXVI / YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy / Flagship 22 of 90 Edition: Research Working Edition v1.0

summary: Coarse flood maps support regional risk assessment but omit terrain detail relevant to local exposure. We present floodsr, a Python framework for reconstructing fine-grid flood depths using a trained residual U-Net (ResUNet) or the existing terrain-based CostGrow method. We trained the terrain-conditioned ResUNet on paired Canadian hydraulic simulations and evaluated it on withheld spatial tiles and independent simulations at two external sites. Wet-loss training improved reconstruction on five selected tiles, although internal validation favoured the deployed baseline. External depth errors decreased, but wet-depth errors and spatial agreement did not improve consistently. CPU benchmarks quantified runtime and memory for both methods, and repeatability and input-validation checks passed in the tested configurations. The framework supports comparison and reuse of reconstruction methods; application-specific validation remains necessary because finer grids do not guarantee more accurate flood maps.   Non-peer-reviewed preprint. Includes the manuscript and supplementary material. Software: https://github.com/cefect/floodsr . Documentation: https://floodsr.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ .

summary: v2.4.1 (2026-10-31) replaces the age-only standardization of v2.4.0 by indirect standardization over 16 sex-by-age strata (KDCA district-by-sex-by-age-band notifications and resident-registration population by district, sex and age band); all arms, threshold refits and figures were rerun and the credible set is unchanged (fiscal independence only). v2.4.0 (revision R1, 2026-10-31) adds revision_R1/: the additional analyses requested at peer review by JMIR Public Health and Surveillance (indirectly age-standardized expected counts as offset; every count or area covariate re-expressed as a share of district land area, a rate per 1000 residents or a density per km2, with log population density added; two uniform functional forms; parsimonious models; restricted spatial regression; zero-inflated negative binomial; residual Moran's I for every specification; 8 neighbourhood graphs; spatially varying coefficients for forest share and household wells; physicians per 1000 as ascertainment proxy; 2022-2024 only; repeated fits; reruns of the complete data pipeline under alternative screening thresholds and with linear interpolation), all outputs, the revised figures, and the inputs needed beyond the raw files. Under the revised principal model only fiscal independence remains credible (IRR 0.890, 95% CrI 0.819-0.966 per SD); the four other associations of the reviewed version survive age standardization alone but not rescaling, and forest share is credible under no revised specification. Three input corrections (Busanjin-gu and Cheonan-si land-use and well values; boundary-file area in place of the sewerage area field; Incheon Michuhol-gu/Namdong-gu polygon assignment) are documented; the reviewed specification refitted on the corrected inputs reproduces its 5 associations. The main script and results/ (v2.3.3, the reviewed analysis) are unchanged. Earlier history: Reproducibility package for a Bayesian spatiotemporal analysis of district-level hepatitis A incidence in South Korea, 2020-2024 (negative binomial, Besag-York-Mollie convolution + RW1 + Knorr-Held Type I interaction, fitted with R-INLA; 219 districts, 1,095 district-years, 27 covariates). v2.1.0 is a DATA-REPAIR release that supersedes all earlier versions: an audit found that several administrative source files store unavailable values as 0 instead of missing and that some series were redefined in particular years, so that, under binary and quantile coding, covariates encoded data availability rather than their true level. These values are now recoded as missing and filled from the most recent earlier available year, and every change is logged (results/data_repair_log.csv). The v2.0.x associations for piped water-supply coverage and inpatient medical cost, and the v2.0.x claim of nine credible covariates, were artefacts of this defect and are withdrawn. The repaired analysis found four credible covariates (household groundwater wells, dairy-cattle farms, forest area, fiscal independence). A post hoc extreme-value screen then found aggregation errors (eg, a sex ratio near 50 males per 100 females, basic livelihood security recipients above 30%, mostly in cities with non-autonomous wards) affecting 17 district-years in 4 covariates; v2.2.0 adopts this screen as rule R7 of the principal analysis, which excludes 2 further districts (218 districts, 1,090 district-years) and adds sewer-pipe repair sites as a fifth credible covariate. Household groundwater wells and sewer-pipe repair sites are borderline (lost under some neighbourhood graphs, INLA settings or the alternative handling of extreme values), and only forest area is credible in every sensitivity analysis; dairy-cattle farms, sewer-pipe repair sites and fiscal independence are lost when 2020-2021 is excluded. The covariates take up only part of the spatial structure (residual Moran's I +0.22). The package contains a single R script (data repair, models, sensitivity and stability analyses), a figure script, a year-R2 data

summary: AUTONOMOUSLY EVOLVING PROGRAMMABLE VEHICLE CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:自主進化可編程車輛文明極限 30/90 AUTONOMOUSLY EVOLVING PROGRAMMABLE VEHICLE CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition in STARLI Research Institute XXXVI and the YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy, Flagship 30 of 90. It asks whether programmable robotic matter and bounded autonomous engineering can generate improved scaled vehicle designs across generations without sacrificing physically verifiable load paths, identity continuity, safe stopping and a later laboratory's right to refute the result. The three-coupling is Programmable Matter x Autonomous Engineering x Cross-Generation Design Evolution. This is a prospective, non-occupancy research program for instrumented material coupons, unoccupied modular bodies and hardware-in-the-loop experiments, not evidence of self-manufacturing roadworthy vehicles. Its falsifiable candidate requires a pre-registered design-evolution method, under the same total material, energy, sensor, computing, operator and testing budgets as capable fixed and classical redesign baselines, to improve independently reproducible successor handoff success without worsening actual structural safety, identity continuity or the complete-denominator rate of severe failures. The source's proposed information-continuity index, I_id = 1 - H(X_t given X_previous,E_t)/H(X_t), is retained as an explicitly conditional information diagnostic rather than physical proof of identity. Blind unlogged module substitutions, weakened joints, sensor-reference drift, changed load spectra, hidden external energy, obsolete signed commands and unsafe intermediate morphing states can refute the claim. Missing load-path, specimen, energy, calibration or stop-authority evidence requires a refusal, not a compensating performance score. Thirty different mathematical plates investigate information continuity, event-hash lineage, physical design transitions, safe feasible sets, material-flow closure, elastic strain energy, structural stiffness and buckling, fatigue crack growth, survival, change-point detection, Bayesian evidence, correlated uncertainty, calibration transfer, safe information gain, held-out generalization, robust risk, Pareto design sets, mutation kernels, quality-diversity coverage, surrogate discrepancy, noninferiority, paired causal effects, selective risk and coverage, physical stop latency, barrier-function constraints, temporal invariants, independent replay frequency and conjunctive release. Each plate provides a mathematical or physical construction, units and scope, a concrete blind refutation and linked chapters; models are not new natural laws or claims of already built systems. Eighty-two chapters and 410 individually paginated studies explore versioned physical lineage, mechanical and thermal design inheritance, feasible design evolution, quality-diversity without safety dilution, fair predecessor comparison, formal assurance, human veto, blind multi-generation experiments and independent successor laboratories. Two hundred Research Gates separately test hidden mechanism failures, matched ancestor-baseline contests and combined cross-chapter counterexamples with individually different measurements, rival explanations and reasons for stopping. Thirty-three distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos propose independent instruments and protocols such as a physical lineage witness, inherited failure library, thermal ancestry panel, independent stopping oscilloscope, proof-to-hardware binding, blinded noninferiority trial, multi-site disagreement archive and a successor's right-to-refute capsule. These are testable future proposals, not completed experimental devices. The DOI evidence ancestry includes author-provided Flagship 13 records 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318839 (formal metadata confirmation required). Method references include Robo-Matter 10.1038/s41467-024-53123-6; formal autonomous-robotic

summary: WARM-RECONFIGURABLE VEHICLES AND COOPERATIVE MOBILITY SYSTEMS AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:群體可重構車輛與協同交通系統極限 29/90 SWARM-RECONFIGURABLE VEHICLES AND COOPERATIVE MOBILITY SYSTEMS AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page high-density English Research Working Edition in the STARLI YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy, Research Institute XXXVI, Flagship 29 of 90. It asks whether a fleet of physically modular, unoccupied scaled vehicles can cooperate in controlled module transfer and transport scheduling without concealing loss of material identity, mechanical safety or human stop authority. Its central three-coupling is Vehicle Cooperation x Module Reconfiguration x Mobility Systems. Physical experiments are proposed only for enclosed small-scale test beds, certified material coupons, hardware-in-the-loop fleet schedules and independently metered docking stations. No integrated public-road vehicle, passenger application, vehicle type approval or automatic nano-to-car scale transfer is asserted. The falsifiable candidate compares a frozen distributed cooperative exchange architecture against competent fixed-body fleet dispatch, centralized modular scheduling and metered teleoperated docking with the same material, energy, operator, station, sensing, communication and computation resources. A proposed service advantage must survive the entire population of requested jobs and attempted exchanges. The source's selective-risk model, R_sel(tau) = E[L(yhat,y) given c >= tau], is retained but always reported together with accepted-task coverage; refusing difficult requests cannot count as safety or efficiency progress. Hidden donated-module withdrawals, false connector capability, overloaded docking, station closures, common-reference localization bias, message partitions, unfair task selection and an unavailable external safety referee are active attempts to refute the central claim. Loss of load path, physically unqualified attachment, forbidden traffic clearance or untraceable authorization is an immediate hard stop. Thirty distinct mathematical research plates develop selective prediction risk and coverage, payload-flow conservation, mixed-integer vehicle-task allocation, authorized discrete topology transitions, headway, time-to-collision, convoy string stability, docking contact impulse, whole-cycle energy conservation, connector shear stress, weak-direction structural stiffness, post-swap center of mass, braking limits, queueing, time-expanded scheduling, graph connectivity, information age, correlated measurement uncertainty, fleet-state inference, robust dispatch and Pareto constraints, causal resource-matched comparisons, component survival, life-cycle emissions and complete-denominator mission yield. Each plate supplies a physical or mathematical construction, units and validity assumptions, a concrete blinded falsifier and linked study chapters. An algorithmic objective does not replace independent mechanical evidence or human authority. Eighty-two chapters and 410 individual single-page research studies examine physical cooperative missions, donor-recipient interfaces, distributed reservations, convoy dynamics, fleet optimization, human supervision, independent metrology and cross-generation research succession. Two hundred Research Gates contain separately formulated concealed failures, strong baseline contests and joint-interface counterexamples, all with specific physical measurands, plausible rival causes, hard-stop conditions and second-laboratory handoff material. Thirty-three distinct Phoenix Answer Embryos propose separate future research instruments and protocols, including a fleet physical-census witness, structural connector transfer kit, independent queue-shock bench, network split-brain referee, calibrated convoy separation track, misidentified energy sensor, and negative-replay capsule. These are independently refutable scientific possibilities, not completed equipment or experimental claims. DOI methodological ancestry includes

It asks whether a fleet of physically modular, unoccupied scaled vehicles can cooperate in controlled module transfer and transport scheduling without concealing loss of material identity, mechanical safety or human stop authority. Its central three-coupling is Vehicle Cooperation x Module Reconfiguration x Mobility Systems. Physical experiments are proposed only for enclosed small-scale test beds, certified material coupons, hardware-in-the-loop fleet schedules and independently metered docking stations. No integrated public-road vehicle, passenger application, vehicle type approval or automatic nano-to-car scale transfer is asserted. The falsifiable candidate compares a frozen distributed cooperative exchange architecture against competent fixed-body fleet dispatch, centralized modular scheduling and metered teleoperated docking with the same material, energy, operator, station, sensing, communication and computation resources. A proposed service advantage must survive the entire population of requested jobs and attempted exchanges. The source's selective-risk model, R_sel(tau) = E[L(yhat,y) given c >= tau], is retained but always reported together with accepted-task coverage; refusing difficult requests cannot count as safety or efficiency progress. Hidden donated-module withdrawals, false connector capability, overloaded docking, station closures, common-reference localization bias, message partitions, unfair task selection and an unavailable external safety referee are active attempts to refute the central claim. Loss of load path, physically unqualified attachment, forbidden traffic clearance or untraceable authorization is an immediate hard stop. Thirty distinct mathematical research plates develop selective prediction risk and coverage, payload-flow conservation, mixed-integer vehicle-task allocation, authorized discrete topology transitions, headway, time-to-collision, convoy string stability, docking contact impulse, whole-cycle energy conservation, connector shear stress, weak-direction structural stiffness, post-swap center of mass, braking limits, queueing, time-expanded scheduling, graph connectivity, information age, correlated measurement uncertainty, fleet-state inference, robust dispatch and Pareto constraints, causal resource-matched comparisons, component survival, life-cycle emissions and complete-denominator mission yield. Each plate supplies a physical or mathematical construction, units and validity assumptions, a concrete blinded falsifier and linked study chapters. An algorithmic objective does not replace independent mechanical evidence or human authority. Eighty-two chapters and 410 individual single-page research studies examine physical cooperative missions, donor-recipient interfaces, distributed reservations, convoy dynamics, fleet optimization, human supervision, independent metrology and cross-generation research succession. Two hundred Research Gates contain separately formulated concealed failures, strong baseline contests and joint-interface counterexamples, all with specific physical measurands, plausible rival causes, hard-stop conditions and second-laboratory handoff material. Thirty-three distinct Phoenix Answer Embryos propose separate future research instruments and protocols, including a fleet physical-census witness, structural connector transfer kit, independent queue-shock bench, network split-brain referee, calibrated convoy separation track, misidentified energy sensor, and negative-replay capsule. These are independently refutable scientific possibilities, not completed equipment or experimental claims. DOI methodological ancestry includes

summary: DIGITAL IDENTITY AND STRUCTURAL CONTINUITY OF MORPHING AUTONOMOUS VEHICLES AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:可變形自主車輛的數位身份與結構連續性極限 28/90 DIGITAL IDENTITY AND STRUCTURAL CONTINUITY OF MORPHING AUTONOMOUS VEHICLES AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition in the STARLI YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy, Research Institute XXXVI, Flagship 28 of 90. It asks whether the identity of a morphing modular vehicle can remain independently reconstructable after authorized component replacement without confusing a valid digital registration with preserved load-bearing structure. The three-way research coupling is Digital Identity x Structural Evolution x Traceability. The scope is unoccupied scaled panels, instrumented materials and hardware-in-the-loop studies; no working road vehicle, human safety certification or legal identity status is claimed. The falsifiable research contract compares a frozen physical-and-digital provenance architecture against conventional fleet records, competent expert inspection and signed digital-twin workflows under equal material, sensor, energy, computing, time and labor budgets. Its principal target is fewer unsafe identity counterexamples without worse independent handoff and replay completeness. summary: TriadSense contains synchronised sensor recordings of nine groups of three people who assembled a puzzle together, with annotations of what every participant, every pair and the whole group did. Each participant wore an ear-worn device (OpenEarable 2.0) and a wrist-worn device (Xsens DOT); an optical motion-capture system (OptiTrack) recorded their positions. The record holds the raw recordings of the nine sessions, the annotations of three annotators (the final annotations, the original annotator's annotations before the review, and the reliability sample of 76 clips), the synchronised streams with the final labels on every sample, and the 5-second window table of the benchmark. Video and audio are not released. README.md describes every file and column. Access to the files requires accepting the terms of use (TERMS_OF_USE.md), which prohibit any attempt to re-identify the participants. The code that reproduces the processing and the benchmark: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/triadsense-pipeline-78DB/
title: TriadSense: body-worn and optical sensing of group activity in triads

summary: TriadSense contains synchronised sensor recordings of nine groups of three people who assembled a puzzle together, with annotations of what every participant, every pair and the whole group did. Each participant wore an ear-worn device (OpenEarable 2.0) and a wrist-worn device (Xsens DOT); an optical motion-capture system (OptiTrack) recorded their positions. The record holds the raw recordings of the nine sessions, the annotations of three annotators (the final annotations, the original annotator's annotations before the review, and the reliability sample of 76 clips), the synchronised streams with the final labels on every sample, and the 5-second window table of the benchmark. Video and audio are not released. README.md describes every file and column. Access to the files requires accepting the terms of use (TERMS_OF_USE.md), which prohibit any attempt to re-identify the participants. The code that reproduces the processing and the benchmark: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/triadsense-pipeline-78DB/

Every figure and table of the article, its Extended Data and its Supplementary Information is produced from the code, input data and results provided here. The Forest Club is a trade-based coalition. Its members hold their forest at its 2019 extent and are deemed compliant with the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR). They charge the forest-risk commodities they import from non-members, either with a flat penalty or with a surcharge proportional to the deforestation embodied in each product. 1. MRIO impact assessment (folders 1. Data and 2. MRIO) The forest-to-cropland and forest-to-pasture transitions of HILDA+ v2.1 (2012–2019) are extracted from the netCDF files and assigned to countries. They are then allocated to the agricultural sectors of the GLORIA MRIO using FAOSTAT harvested areas and livestock numbers, smoothed with three-year moving averages; the FAO–GLORIA mapping and the hectares per head are in A-1_FAO_Cropland_mapping_GLORIA.xlsx and A-2_Head_per_ha.xlsx. Consumption-based accounting (CBA) attributes this agricultural deforestation to final consumers. Throughflow-based accounting (TBA, by hypothetical extraction) traces the share that transits through intermediary economies such as the EU, in detail for Brazil, Indonesia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The folders hold the Python script (CBA_TBA_script.py), the Alteryx workflows, the satellite accounts, the results and the visualisation files (Tableau, Sankey diagrams). These produce sections 2–4 of the Supplementary Information (Tables S1–S2, Figs S1–S4), which describe the deforestation the EUDR covers. 2. CGE model (synced from GitHub) The study simulates how the club forms, round by round, as each country compares its welfare inside and outside it. The model is GTAP-AEZ, a global CGE model with agro-ecological zones (42 regions, 35 sectors, 18 zones; GEMPACK). Every result is measured against a baseline that combines the EUDR with the business-as-usual clearing that DeDuCE v2.1 attributes to agriculture. The coalitions reached are tested for one-country deviations and for their sensitivity to the switching cost. 0_External_data: footprint intensities and border charges derived from DeDuCE v2.1, the EUDR import cut shares, the business-as-usual clearing by region and agro-ecological zone (HILDA+ v2.1 patterns; MapBiomas RAD 2025 for Brazil), and the productivity calibration of the cleared land. 1_Code: R scripts that calibrate and solve the two-stage baseline, run the membership game and the one-deviation stability tests, and calibrate the land-supply elasticities to Miranda et al. (2024). 2_Model: the GTAP-AEZ model files (TABLO code, command files, sets and aggregation). 3_Output and 4_DB: the text outputs of every solve and the result tables of every run, by region and round, for all membership processes and stability tests of the paper. 5_Figures: the Python pipeline that redraws all figures and tables from these results, with their source data. Data not included The GTAP Data Base (version 12, reference year 2019) is licensed by the Center for Global Trade Analysis, Purdue University. Solving the model requires a licensed copy in 2_Model/in/. Redrawing the figures and tables does not, because the extracted results are provided in 5_Figures/data. The GLORIA tables are distributed by the Global MRIO Lab. The README of the repository describes each step of the CGE pipeline. Code synced from the GitHub repository: https://github.com/etiennebert/forest_club/tree/main
title: A Trade-Based Forest Club as a Path to Halting Tropical Deforestation

[ 1 , 2 ] Ecco come si collegano questi tre elementi:   1. La prima battaglia del Monte Emo (335 a.C.) Prima di lanciare la sua campagna contro i Persiani, Alessandro Magno guidò una spedizione nei Balcani per rendere sicuri i confini settentrionali del suo regno. Sul Monte Emo (l'attuale catena dei Monti Balcani) affrontò i Traci Liberi e altre tribù locali. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] La tattica dei carri: I Traci si erano posizionati sulla vetta e intendevano far rotolare dei pesanti carri giù dai ripidi pendii per rompere la falange macedone. [ 1 , 2 ] La contromossa di Alessandro: Il re macedone ordinò ai suoi soldati di aprire i ranghi per far passare i carri oppure di sdraiarsi a terra coprendosi con gli scudi intersecati (creando una sorta di testuggine). La tattica funzionò alla perfezione: i carri rimbalzarono sugli scudi senza causare vittime tra i Macedoni. Le truppe di Alessandro caricarono poi la vetta, sbaragliando i difensori. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]   2. Lo scontro dei Bessi con Roma (72 a.C.) In epoca successiva, il nome della battaglia del Monte Emo si associa alla sottomissione definitiva dei Bessi , una delle tribù tracie più bellicose e fanaticamente dedite al culto religioso. Il proconsole romano Marco Licinio Lucullo affrontò i Bessi proprio nei pressi della catena del Monte Emo, sconfiggendoli duramente in una grande battaglia campale, conquistando il loro centro principale ( Uscudama ) e aprendo la strada alla successiva egemonia romana nella regione. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]   3. Il legame con Perperikon La tribù dei Bessi era storicamente la custode del famosissimo Santuario e Oracolo di Dioniso , situato proprio sulla maestosa roccia sacra di Perperikon . Questo luogo ha un valore storico eccezionale per due importanti profezie collegate ai protagonisti di queste guerre: [ 1 , 2 ] La profezia di Alessandro Magno: Secondo le fonti antiche, prima di iniziare la sua spedizione in Asia (subito dopo aver pacificato la Tracia), Alessandro visitò l'oracolo di Dioniso a Perperikon. Il vino versato sull'altare creò una fiammata altissima fino al cielo, un segno divino che i sacerdoti interpretarono come il presagio che avrebbe conquistato il mondo intero. [ 1 ] La profezia di Ottaviano Augusto: Anni dopo, anche il padre di Augusto (Gaio Ottavio) ricevette nello stesso santuario dei Bessi la medesima profezia sul futuro dominio globale di suo figlio. [ 1 ] In sintesi, la resistenza dei Traci sul Monte Emo rappresenta lo scontro militare per il controllo dei Balcani, mentre Perperikon costituisce il cuore
title: ROMA CONTRO SARDEGNA: Roma dovette disintegrare l'impero sardo pezzo per pezzo con singole guerre da Divide et Impera

Sul Monte Emo (l'attuale catena dei Monti Balcani) affrontò i Traci Liberi e altre tribù locali. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] La tattica dei carri: I Traci si erano posizionati sulla vetta e intendevano far rotolare dei pesanti carri giù dai ripidi pendii per rompere la falange macedone. [ 1 , 2 ] La contromossa di Alessandro: Il re macedone ordinò ai suoi soldati di aprire i ranghi per far passare i carri oppure di sdraiarsi a terra coprendosi con gli scudi intersecati (creando una sorta di testuggine). La tattica funzionò alla perfezione: i carri rimbalzarono sugli scudi senza causare vittime tra i Macedoni. Le truppe di Alessandro caricarono poi la vetta, sbaragliando i difensori. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]   2. Lo scontro dei Bessi con Roma (72 a.C.) In epoca successiva, il nome della battaglia del Monte Emo si associa alla sottomissione definitiva dei Bessi , una delle tribù tracie più bellicose e fanaticamente dedite al culto religioso. Il proconsole romano Marco Licinio Lucullo affrontò i Bessi proprio nei pressi della catena del Monte Emo, sconfiggendoli duramente in una grande battaglia campale, conquistando il loro centro principale ( Uscudama ) e aprendo la strada alla successiva egemonia romana nella regione. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]   3. Il legame con Perperikon La tribù dei Bessi era storicamente la custode del famosissimo Santuario e Oracolo di Dioniso , situato proprio sulla maestosa roccia sacra di Perperikon . Questo luogo ha un valore storico eccezionale per due importanti profezie collegate ai protagonisti di queste guerre: [ 1 , 2 ] La profezia di Alessandro Magno: Secondo le fonti antiche, prima di iniziare la sua spedizione in Asia (subito dopo aver pacificato la Tracia), Alessandro visitò l'oracolo di Dioniso a Perperikon. Il vino versato sull'altare creò una fiammata altissima fino al cielo, un segno divino che i sacerdoti interpretarono come il presagio che avrebbe conquistato il mondo intero. [ 1 ] La profezia di Ottaviano Augusto: Anni dopo, anche il padre di Augusto (Gaio Ottavio) ricevette nello stesso santuario dei Bessi la medesima profezia sul futuro dominio globale di suo figlio. [ 1 ] In sintesi, la resistenza dei Traci sul Monte Emo rappresenta lo scontro militare per il controllo dei Balcani, mentre Perperikon costituisce il cuore

summary: Anonymized deposit for double-blind peer review. It contains the MI-Snow1000 lane-detection dataset: 4,888 annotated frames in TuSimple format, both split definitions, the per-frame condition tags, the trained checkpoints in PyTorch and ONNX form, each model's predictions from three training runs, the evaluation scripts, and a browsable annotated sample. The checkpoints are trained on the training partition of the sequence-disjoint split, and tools/eval/score_benchmark.py reproduces the benchmark tables of the paper from the included predictions. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Author attribution and a permanent DOI will be added at camera-ready.

summary: Replication package for a study of commit records in public GitHub Classroom repositories (58,516 repositories collected in August 2026, shortly before GitHub retired Classroom). It contains the collection, extraction, and analysis scripts; hashed derived tables at the commit and repository level; the result file of every analysis; the LaTeX source of the manuscript; an entry point that rebuilds the generated tables, figures, and text numbers from the result files, re-fits from the derived tables the models of the main comparisons and of their variants, and checks the numbers typed into the manuscript; the preregistered protocol and its results; the post-registration decision log (D1 to D10, E1 to E15); and a log of generative-AI use. Raw commit logs and a manual-review file containing commit text are not distributed.
title: GitHub Classroom commit records before and after generative AI: replication package (activity attribution, platform change, organization weighting)
